matrices-s2.title: A food truck's weekend

table.caption: Number of items a food truck sold on two days, and the price of each item in dollars

matrices-s2.text: Let $Q = \left[ \begin{matrix} 40 & 65 & 90 \\ 55 & 50 & 70 \end{matrix} \right]$ hold the sales and $P = \left[ \begin{matrix} 6 \\ 3 \\ 2 \end{matrix} \right]$ the prices.

options: Row times column for each of the four entries.
This is $BA$; the order is reversed.
This multiplies entries in matching positions; use rows times columns.

items.q: What is the entry in row 1, column 2 of $BA$?

mistakes.why: That entry belongs to $AB$. For $BA$ use row 1 of $B$, $(2, 0)$, and column 2 of $A$, $(-1, 2)$.
That is row 2, column 1. Row 1 of $B$ times column 2 of $A$: $2(-1) + 0(2)$.

items.q: Which products are defined? Select all that apply.

why.correct: $A$ and $B$ are $2 \times 2$; $C$ is $2 \times 3$. A product needs the inside numbers to match.

options: Rows come first: $A$ has $2$ rows, $C$ has $3$ columns.
$C$ has $3$ columns, so the product does too.
$A$ has $2$ rows, so the product does too.

items.q: What is the entry in row 2, column 1 of $AC$?

mistakes.why: That is row 1, column 1. Use row 2 of $A$, $(1, 2)$.
Pair first with first and second with second: $1(1) + 2(3)$.

items.q: What was Saturday's revenue, in dollars?

mistakes.why: $195$ counts items sold. Multiply each count by its price: $40(6) + 65(3) + 90(2)$.
$11$ adds the prices. Multiply each price by how many were sold, then add.

items.q: Which product gives both days' revenues at once?

why.correct: $Q$ is $2 \times 3$ and $P$ is $3 \times 1$: $QP$ is defined and is $2 \times 1$, one revenue per day.
options: $PQ$ is $(3 \times 1)(2 \times 3)$: inside $1 \ne 2$, so it is not defined.

items.q: What was Sunday's revenue, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is Saturday. Use row 2 of $Q$.

items.q: If every price rises by \$1, by how many dollars does Saturday's revenue increase?

mistakes.why: Each item sold brings in \$1 more, so the increase is the number of items sold: $40 + 65 + 90$.
$810$ is the new revenue. The question asks for the increase, $810 - 615$.

why.correct: Each item sold now brings in one more dollar, so the increase is $40(1) + 65(1) + 90(1) = 195$ dollars, the number of items sold on Saturday.
Two rows and three columns: $2 \times 3$, rows first.
options: Rows come first: there are $2$ rows.
Count rows and columns, not entries.

items.q: Which matrix $I$ satisfies $AI = A$ for every $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$?

why.correct: The identity matrix has $1$s on the main diagonal and $0$s elsewhere. Check: $\left[ \begin{matrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{matrix} \right]\left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{matrix} \right]$.
options: This adds the columns together: $a + b$ appears in both columns.
This swaps the two columns of $A$.
This replaces the second column of $A$ with zeros.

items.q: For two matrices, $AB = \left[ \begin{matrix} 4 & 7 \\ -6 & 3 \end{matrix} \right]$ and $BA = \left[ \begin{matrix} 2 & 11 \\ -4 & 5 \end{matrix} \right]$. What does this show?
options: The order of the factors in a matrix product matters
One of the two products was computed wrongly
Matrix multiplication is the same as entrywise multiplication

why.correct: Both products exist and are $2 \times 2$, yet they differ: matrix multiplication is not commutative.
options: Different results are expected; for matrices $AB$ and $BA$ usually differ.
Both products are $2 \times 2$, so $A$ and $B$ are both $2 \times 2$.
Entrywise multiplication would give the same result in either order.
Every entry is multiplied, not only the first.
This multiplies matching positions ($1 \cdot 5$ and $4 \cdot (-1)$); use whole rows.
This uses columns of the first matrix instead of rows.
The product is $2 \times 1$, a column, not a row.

items.q: Write the top entry of $\left[ \begin{matrix} k & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{matrix} \right]\left[ \begin{matrix} k \\ 4 \end{matrix} \right]$ as an expression in $k$.

mistakes.why: Multiply the $1$ by the $4$ below it: $1 \cdot 4 = 4$.
That is the bottom entry, row 2 times the column.

why.correct: Row 1, $(k, 1)$, times the column $(k, 4)$: $k \cdot k + 1 \cdot 4 = k^2 + 4$.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the entry in row $i$, column $j$ of $AB$ in order.
options: Check that the columns of $A$ match the rows of $B$
Take row $i$ of $A$ and column $j$ of $B$

why.correct: First make sure the product exists, then pair a row with a column, multiply pairwise and add.
